w: What's tested Occlusal trauma: the definition, and primary vs secondary (normal vs reduced support); the difference is clinical, not histologic Unilateral vs jiggling forces, and the hourglass The signs: clinical (fremitus and the rest) and radiographic (a widened PDL and the rest); a vertical defect doesn't mean occlusal trauma Mobility: what it depends on, what causes it, how it's graded, and why it's a sign of adaptation What the animal experiments showed: trauma alone, trauma with gingivitis, trauma with periodontitis Occlusal discrepancies and occlusal adjustment: what it does and doesn't do, and when to do it His conclusions, the bottom line 1 His conclusions: occlusal trauma doesn't cause gingivitis or periodontitis; no human evidence it speeds attachment loss A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Know this His bottom line: trauma doesn't cause gingivitis or periodontitis, but it affects the supporting tissues. Occlusal trauma does not cause gingivitis or periodontitis. It does affect the supporting periodontal tissues: "absolutely yes." There is a lack of evidence from human studies implicating occlusal trauma in the progression of attachment loss in periodontitis (the only evidence came from one group's animal studies). 2 Occlusal trauma is the injury, not the force; primary vs secondary: normal vs reduced support; the same histologically; the fence post A professor's hint · 8 questions in the bank Know this Primary: traumatic forces on normal support (no bone or attachment lost). Secondary: normal or traumatic forces on reduced support. The fence post: less of it in the ground, the same lean tips it. The forces Traumatic (excessive) occlusal forces Normal or traumatic occlusal forces The support Normal: normal bone level, normal attachment level Reduced: bone loss and attachment loss already present In short The tooth hasn't lost a single millimeter of attachment or bone Even a normal force can injure a tooth that has lost support Why can a normal force injure a tooth with reduced support? With normal support, the tooth's center of rotation is generally in the mid-root; with reduced support it moves apically, toward the apical third. His analogy is the fence post: with two thirds of it in the ground, lean on it and it probably won't move; with only a third, or 20%, in the ground, the same lean (same force, same mass, same everything) may tip it over. 3 Trauma alone, and with gingivitis: mobility and bone density loss, no attachment loss, reversible A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Occlusal trauma alone (both groups) Increased mobility; loss of bone density (more radiolucent, but no loss of crestal bone height); no loss of attachment; a return to pretreatment stability once the trauma was removed Trauma plus inflammation on a normal periodontium (gingivitis) Increased mobility; greater loss of bone density; still no attachment loss Trauma plus inflammation on a reduced periodontium (periodontitis) The groups disagreed. Beagle dogs: attachment and bone loss beyond what the disease caused alone ("co-destruction is a reality"). Squirrel monkeys: no further attachment loss beyond the disease alone ("co-destruction is a question") 4 Occlusal adjustment: what it does and doesn't do, and when (after the inflammation is treated, unless acute) A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Adjust the occlusion after treating the inflammation (at re-evaluation), unless it's acute, like fremitus at the first exam. Adjustment helps mobility and bone, but only plaque control stops the disease. Treat the infection first, then adjust (an adjunct, like antibiotics). Except in acute conditions, occlusion is addressed during initial therapy, after efforts to reduce or minimize the inflammatory lesion. An acute condition is, for example, fremitus or a heavily loaded tooth at the first exam: then he might adjust the occlusion early. Otherwise, start with the usual periodontal treatment (oral hygiene instructions, scaling and root planing, the rest of phase 1), keep monitoring the teeth you suspect have occlusal trauma throughout therapy, and at the phase 1 re-evaluation, adjust the occlusion if they haven't improved with periodontal treatment alone. Occlusal adjustment may reduce the mobility of traumatized teeth and promote the regrowth of bone, but it will not arrest the breakdown caused by plaque. You still have to control the plaque. When it's done, adjusting occlusal discrepancies should follow successful anti-infective periodontal therapy. Like antibiotics (Dr. Litz's lecture), it's not where you start: treat the inflammation first, then adjust the occlusion if there's still room for it. 5 The signs: confirmed only histologically; fremitus; a widened PDL (about 0.25 mm); a vertical defect isn't proof A professor's hint · 11 questions in the bank Know this Confirmed only histologically; the signs are surrogates. A diagnosis, not a finding. Fremitus: the patient taps, a finger on the facial gingiva feels the tooth move. Not a mobility grade, but usually a Class 3 tooth. Occlusal trauma can only be confirmed histologically, and we don't do histology on patients. The clinical and radiographic findings are surrogate indicators of it. In the slides' words, "occlusal trauma" is a diagnosis, not a finding. Fremitus: a palpable or visible movement of a tooth when subjected to occlusal forces, sometimes called functional mobility. To test it, have the patient tap their teeth together while you rest a finger on the facial gingiva: if you feel the tooth move under your finger, it is being pushed every time the teeth meet. When it's advanced you can see it without a finger. It shows mostly on anterior teeth. Fremitus isn't part of the mobility classification, but a tooth with fremitus usually has Class 3 mobility. A widened PDL space. In health the space is roughly 0.25 mm; a wider radiolucent band around the tooth suggests the tooth is likely mobile (confirm it clinically), under forces that shift it in more than one direction. 6 Mobility: what it depends on and what causes it; the grades; adaptation; mobile teeth heal less well A professor's hint · 10 questions in the bank Know this Mobile teeth heal less well: bring a Class 2 tooth to Class 1 or less by adjusting the occlusion if you can. 0 Physiologic mobility, 0.1-0.2 mm horizontally: no movement you can see 1 Increased mobility of the crown, at most 1 mm horizontally 2 Visibly increased mobility, more than 1 mm horizontally 3 Severe: horizontal and vertical (press on the occlusal surface and it moves up into the socket), impinging on function Mobile teeth respond less well to treatment, whether regenerative treatment or soft tissue grafting. Class 1 doesn't affect it as much as Class 2, so for a Class 2 tooth, adjust the occlusion to bring it to Class 1 or less, if you can. In the slides' words (Lindhe and Ericsson): permanent increased mobility has no influence on the development of periodontal disease, but healing after periodontal treatment may be better in non-mobile than in mobile teeth. 7 Trauma with periodontitis: the animal groups disagreed; stopping the trauma doesn't reverse periodontitis A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Know this Stopping the trauma doesn't reverse periodontitis: treat the periodontitis. Co-destruction (Glickman): plaque inflammation alone stays in the zone of irritation (the marginal and interdental gingiva) and causes gingivitis, and its spread leads to horizontal bone loss. Traumatic occlusion acts on the zone of co-destruction (the PDL, the alveolar bone and the cementum; in class he included the transseptal fibers, which the slides draw as the boundary between the zones) and changes the pathway of the inflammation into it, giving vertical defects. Occlusion is a co-destructive factor added to the bacterial insult. In the monkeys, 10 weeks after the trauma stopped, the bone regained its density. But 10 weeks after stopping the trauma without treating the periodontitis, there was no return to stability: stopping the occlusal trauma does not reverse periodontitis. You still have to treat the periodontitis. 8 Jiggling vs unilateral forces: the hourglass A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Know this Jiggling forces: from both sides, an hourglass-shaped widening of the PDL. Orthodontics uses a controlled unilateral force. A unilateral force acts in one direction: pressure on one side and tension on the other. Orthodontics uses it: tipping (the crown leans, mesially or distally, to position the tooth in the arch) or bodily movement (the whole tooth, root and crown, moves in one direction). Orthodontics does controlled, unilateral movement, not jiggling. A jiggling force comes from one side and then from the other: once from the mesial and once from the distal, or once from the facial and once from the lingual. Because the tooth is pushed both ways, there is pressure and tension on both sides, and the net result is an hourglass shape around the tooth: a widened PDL, bone loss on both sides, and mobility. The slides call this "often the clinical situation in humans." 9 Occlusal discrepancies: a CR-to-CO slide over 1 mm, non-working contacts; not every one needs adjusting Core of the slides · 5 questions in the bank The randomized trial (often cited to justify what we do): 50 patients with periodontitis, randomly assigned to occlusal adjustment or none, and all of them got all the periodontal treatment they needed, non-surgical or surgical. After two years, the adjusted group had a better gain in clinical attachment (about 0.5 mm) but no difference in probing depth. Attachment gain held over time says something about long-term healing, where a drop in probing depth can come from the tissue shrinking after a good SRP. Initial mobility, Class 1 or Class 2, didn't affect the result. Two camps remain. For adjustment: that trial, and a study in which teeth with occlusal discrepancies had deeper initial probing depths, more mobility and poorer prognoses than teeth without. Careful patient selection: not every occlusal discrepancy causes occlusal trauma, so not every discrepancy in a patient with periodontitis needs to be adjusted. That camp doesn't say never adjust; it says choose who gets adjusted. 10 Overload and surgery as causes of mobility: a high crown; up to a year after a flap Core of the lecture · 4 questions in the bank Overloading, or occlusal trauma: a Class II, an MOD or a crown left high, so the tooth is the first contact every time the patient closes. It may become uncomfortable or painful on biting, and it will become mobile. Periodontal surgery: after a flap on a quadrant (resective surgery), expect the teeth to be slightly mobile for up to a year; they settle down. 11 The gingiva's blood supply (supraperiosteal), and the old idea that occlusion caused periodontitis Core of the slides · 3 questions in the bank Perfusion studies refuted that: the gingiva's blood supply is external to the alveolus. It has three sources: the PDL arteries, the intra-alveolar arteries through the bone, and the supraperiosteal arteries, the main supply to the marginal gingiva. Also flagged in class Occlusal trauma is the injury, not the force: the force starts it, the tissue changes in the periodontium are the trauma. Primary vs secondary is clinical; histologically the same. Radiographic signs: a widened PDL (normal about 0.25 mm), a thickened or discontinued lamina dura, bone loss, root resorption. A vertical defect doesn't mean occlusal trauma (trauma with bone loss tends to be vertical, not the reverse). Mobility can be adaptation: find out why. Class 2 isn't hopeless; Class 3 is much worse. Animals, trauma alone: mobility and less dense bone, no attachment loss, reversible once stopped. Not a primary factor. Trauma alone: bone resorbs in density, not height, and it reverses once the force is gone.
